steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a computer vision paper on our method ArGue, attribute-guided prompt tuning for vision-language models. Motivate it with visual attributes and shortcut learning, introduce the main components, and summarize what the experiments show.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Soft prompt tuning for adapting V&L models
- Visual attributes help zero-shot recognition
- Problem: shortcuts / wrong rationales in V&L models
- ArGue: attribute-guided prompt tuning
- Attribute Sampling
- Negative Prompting (ArGue-N)
- Summary of results and aim

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Soft prompt tuning
  - increasingly favored for adapting V&L models (cite) to downstream tasks (cite)
  - few soft tokens: parity with or better than full fine-tuning
  - new task = prompt replacement, not big model reconfiguration (cite)

- Visual attributes
  - classification prompt tuning: learnable context before class name (cite)
  - zero-shot recognition work: adding visual attributes describing classes to input helps (cite)
  - class names (\rm cat, \rm bird) = high-level semantics; primitive attributes (\rm long\ tail, \rm black\ paw) = more precise at inference
  - big zero-shot accuracy gain; insight for transfer learning, esp. few-shot

- Shortcuts in V&L models
  - adapt easily but often incorrect rationales (cite)
  - example: bird in the sky classified via spurious bird-sky correlation, not semantics
  - models highlighting spurious correlations (background) generalize poorly OOD

- ArGue
  - vanilla prompt tuning: align image features with class names
  - ArGue: high confidence on visual attributes generated by LLMs (cite)
  - recognizing primitive attributes = correct rationales, not spurious correlations
  - advantages: attributes from class names only avoid image shortcuts; attributes shared across classes -> generalization

- Attribute Sampling
  - quality of LLM attributes uncertain even with careful prompting
  - select representative, non-redundant attributes aligned with images
  - cluster attribute pool; per cluster rank by image similarity in feature space, keep most correlated
  - 80% fewer attributes -> better accuracy, less compute

- Negative Prompting (ArGue-N)
  - negative attribute: no class semantics, activates spurious correlations -> model should favor no class
  - general negative prompt {\rm the\ background\ of\ a\ \{class\}}; attribute activates image background
  - enforce uniform predictive distribution (Fig. 1)
  - weak assumption, but consistent OOD gains

- Summary
  - attributes -> correct rationales -> robustness in transfer learning
  - beats SOTA prompt tuning; first to surpass pre-trained models on 10 of 11 datasets in novel class accuracy
  - consistently better OOD generalization
  - aim: foundational reference, strong baseline

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Soft prompt tuning is becoming more and more popular as a way to let Vision-Language (V&L) models be adapted efficiently to downstream tasks. With only a few soft tokens, models can reach the same performance as fully fine-tuned ones, and sometimes they even do better. Also, when we adapt to a different downstream task we usually only need to replace the prompt instead of reconfiguring the model a lot, which is another reason why soft prompt tuning is superior.

For a typical classification task, prompt tuning usually means putting a learnable context directly before the class name. But recent work on zero-shot recognition has shown that there are big benefits if visual attributes that describe the classes are added into the input. Class names like \rm cat or \rm bird capture high-level semantics, but at inference time primitive attributes like \rm long\ tail or \rm black\ paw give a more precise specification. Adding them improves zero-shot classification accuracy a lot, and this gives some insight for transfer learning, especially in the few-shot setting.

In this paper we look at visual attributes for transfer learning. We do this by identifying shortcuts that exist in V&L models. These models adapt easily to new tasks, but they often give the wrong rationales for their decisions. For example, a V&L model might classify an object in the sky correctly as a bird, but not because it understands the semantic features, rather because it picks up a spurious correlation between the bird and the sky. If a model mostly highlights spurious correlations, like the background, it has trouble generalizing well to out-of-distribution data.

To deal with this we introduce Attribute-Guided Prompt Tuning (ArGue). The vanilla prompt tuning methods align image features directly with class names. Instead, ArGue encourages the model to be highly confident in recognizing the associated visual attributes, which are generated by Large Language Models (LLMs). The idea is that if a model can identify these primitive attributes, it has captured the correct rationales for a class and is not being influenced by spurious correlations. There are two key advantages. First, the attributes are generated only from class names, so they naturally avoid the shortcuts that are present in images. Second, these primitive attributes can be shared by other classes, which helps the generalization of the model.

- Attribute Sampling
  - quality of LLM attributes uncertain even with careful prompting
  - select representative, non-redundant attributes aligned with images
  - cluster attribute pool; per cluster rank by image similarity in feature space, keep most correlated
  - 80% fewer attributes -> better accuracy, less compute

- Negative Prompting (ArGue-N)
  - negative attribute: no class semantics, activates spurious correlations -> model should favor no class
  - general negative prompt {\rm the\ background\ of\ a\ \{class\}}; attribute activates image background
  - enforce uniform predictive distribution (Fig. 1)
  - weak assumption, but consistent OOD gains

- Summary
  - attributes -> correct rationales -> robustness in transfer learning
  - beats SOTA prompt tuning; first to surpass pre-trained models on 10 of 11 datasets in novel class accuracy
  - consistently better OOD generalization
  - aim: foundational reference, strong baseline

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Soft prompt tuning is becoming more and more popular as a way to let Vision-Language (V&L) models be adapted efficiently to downstream tasks. With only a few soft tokens, models can reach the same performance as fully fine-tuned ones, and sometimes they even do better. Also, when we adapt to a different downstream task we usually only need to replace the prompt instead of reconfiguring the model a lot, which is another reason why soft prompt tuning is superior.

For a typical classification task, prompt tuning usually means putting a learnable context directly before the class name. But recent work on zero-shot recognition has shown that there are big benefits if visual attributes that describe the classes are added into the input. Class names like \rm cat or \rm bird capture high-level semantics, but at inference time primitive attributes like \rm long\ tail or \rm black\ paw give a more precise specification. Adding them improves zero-shot classification accuracy a lot, and this gives some insight for transfer learning, especially in the few-shot setting.

In this paper we look at visual attributes for transfer learning. We do this by identifying shortcuts that exist in V&L models. These models adapt easily to new tasks, but they often give the wrong rationales for their decisions. For example, a V&L model might classify an object in the sky correctly as a bird, but not because it understands the semantic features, rather because it picks up a spurious correlation between the bird and the sky. If a model mostly highlights spurious correlations, like the background, it has trouble generalizing well to out-of-distribution data.

To deal with this we introduce Attribute-Guided Prompt Tuning (ArGue). The vanilla prompt tuning methods align image features directly with class names. Instead, ArGue encourages the model to be highly confident in recognizing the associated visual attributes, which are generated by Large Language Models (LLMs). The idea is that if a model can identify these primitive attributes, it has captured the correct rationales for a class and is not being influenced by spurious correlations. There are two key advantages. First, the attributes are generated only from class names, so they naturally avoid the shortcuts that are present in images. Second, these primitive attributes can be shared by other classes, which helps the generalization of the model.

However, even with careful prompting, the quality of the attributes generated directly from LLMs is still uncertain. So we present Attribute Sampling, which selects the most representative and non-redundant attributes that align well with the corresponding images. In particular, we cluster the attribute pool, so that we can pick the most representative attributes in each cluster and avoid redundancy. Then inside each cluster we rank the attributes by their similarity to the images in the feature space and choose the ones that are most closely correlated. In this way the most semantically relevant visual attributes for the images get selected. In our experiments we see that reducing the number of attributes by 80% overall actually improves accuracy, and it also saves computational resources.

In addition, building on attribute-guided prompt tuning, we introduce Negative Prompting, i.e., ArGue-N. Our argument is that when the model is given a negative attribute, meaning one that has no class-specific semantics and that activates spurious correlations, it should not favor any class. We give a general negative prompt, i.e., {\rm the\ background\ of\ a\ \{class\}}, where the attribute {\rm the\ background\ of\ a} activates the background of the images, which is semantically unrelated to the classes. When a negative prompt is used, we force the model to have a uniform predictive probability distribution (Fig. 1 shows an illustration of negative prompting). Even though the general negative prompt is only a weak assumption, we see consistent performance improvements on out-of-distribution datasets.

To sum up, our research is about using visual attributes to make models understand the correct rationales, which improves robustness for transfer learning. In the experiments our method does better than existing state-of-the-art prompt tuning methods, and for the first time it surpasses the pre-trained models on 10 out of 11 benchmark datasets in novel class accuracy. Our method also shows consistently better out-of-distribution generalization than the baselines. We hope our work can be a foundational reference for using attributes in transfer learning and a strong baseline for the research community.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Soft prompt tuning is increasingly favored for enabling Vision-Language (V&L) models [1,2,3] to be efficiently adapted to downstream tasks [4,5,6]. Models with a few soft tokens can match, or even outperform, fully fine-tuned ones. Moreover, adapting to different downstream tasks typically requires only prompt replacement rather than extensive model reconfiguration [7,8], which further explains the superiority of soft prompt tuning.

In typical classification tasks, prompt tuning often introduces a learnable context directly before the class name [5]. However, recent research in zero-shot recognition has emphasized the substantial benefits of incorporating into the input visual attributes that describe the classes [9,10,11,12,13]. Although class names, e.g., \rm cat or \rm bird, capture high-level semantics, primitive attributes, e.g., \rm long\ tail or \rm black\ paw, provide a more precise specification during inference. This augmentation significantly improves zero-shot classification accuracy and offers insights into transfer learning, particularly in few-shot scenarios.

In this paper, we investigate visual attributes for transfer learning by identifying the shortcuts that exist in V&L models, which adapt easily to new tasks but often provide incorrect rationales for their decisions [15]. For instance, a V&L model may correctly classify an object in the sky as a bird, not because it comprehends the semantic features, but because it detects spurious correlations between the bird and the sky. A model that mainly highlights spurious correlations, e.g., the background, struggles to generalize to out-of-distribution data.

To mitigate this challenge, we introduce Attribute-Guided Prompt Tuning (ArGue). Unlike vanilla prompt tuning methods, which directly align image features with class names, ArGue encourages models to express high confidence in recognizing associated visual attributes generated by Large Language Models (LLMs) [16,17,18]. The underlying idea is that a model able to identify these primitive attributes captures the correct rationales for a class instead of being influenced by spurious correlations. This approach has two key advantages: first, attributes generated solely from class names naturally avoid the shortcuts present in images; second, these primitive attributes may be shared by other classes, which enhances the model's generalization capability.

Nevertheless, despite careful prompting, the quality of attributes generated directly from LLMs remains uncertain. To address this, we present Attribute Sampling, which selects the most representative and non-redundant attributes that align well with the corresponding images. Specifically, the attribute pool is clustered so that the most representative attributes can be selected per cluster while avoiding redundancy. Then, within each cluster, we rank attributes by their similarity to images in the feature space and keep the most closely correlated ones. This process selects the most semantically relevant visual attributes for the images. Empirically, reducing the number of attributes by 80% overall improves accuracy while also saving computational resources.

Furthermore, building on attribute-guided prompt tuning, we introduce Negative Prompting, i.e., ArGue-N. We argue that when presented with a negative attribute, one that carries no class-specific semantics and activates spurious correlations, the model should not favor any class. We provide a general negative prompt, i.e., {\rm the\ background\ of\ a\ \{class\}}, where the attribute {\rm the\ background\ of\ a} activates the background of images, which is semantically unrelated to the classes. When a negative prompt is employed, we enforce a uniform predictive probability distribution for the model (see Fig. 1 for an illustration of negative prompting). Despite the weak assumption behind the general negative prompt, we observe consistent performance gains on out-of-distribution datasets.

In summary, our research focuses on leveraging visual attributes to encourage models to comprehend correct rationales, thereby improving robustness in transfer learning. Experiments show that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art prompt tuning methods and, for the first time, surpasses pre-trained models on 10 out of 11 benchmark datasets in novel class accuracy. Our method also shows consistently superior out-of-distribution generalization compared with baselines. We hope our work can serve as a foundational reference for applying attributes in transfer learning and provide a strong baseline for the research community.
